abstract.text:
As a promising branch of robotics, imitation learning emerges as an important way to transfer human skills to
robots, where human demonstrations represented in Cartesian
or joint spaces are utilized to estimate task/skill models that can
be subsequently generalized to new situations. While learning
Cartesian positions suffices for many applications, the endeffector orientation is required in many others. Despite recent
advances in learning orientations from demonstrations, several
crucial issues have not been adequately addressed yet. For
instance, how can demonstrated orientations be adapted to pass
through arbitrary desired points that comprise orientations and
angular velocities? In this paper, we propose an approach that is
capable of learning multiple orientation trajectories and adapting
learned orientation skills to new situations (e.g., via-points and
end-points), where both orientation and angular velocity are
considered. Specifically, we introduce a kernelized treatment
to alleviate explicit basis functions when learning orientations,
which allows for learning orientation trajectories associated with
high-dimensional inputs. In addition, we extend our approach
to the learning of quaternions with angular acceleration or jerk
constraints, which allows for generating smoother orientation
profiles for robots. Several examples including experiments with
real 7-DoF robot arms are provided to verify the effectiveness of
our method.

sections.summary: Imitation learning is promising for transferring human skills to robots, but Cartesian orientation learning remains difficult because quaternions must obey constraints and must support via-point/end-point adaptation, angular velocities, high-dimensional inputs, and smoothness. The paper positions an analytical solution against prior work and summarizes its contributions in Table I.

N many challenging tasks (e.g., robot table tennis [2] and bimanual manipulation [3]), it is non-trivial to manually define proper trajectories for robots beforehand, hence imitation learning is suggested in order to facilitate the transfer of human skills to robots [4].

As suggested in [7], [22], the probability distribution of multiple demonstrations often encapsulates important motion features and further facilitates the design of optimal controllers [11], [23], [24], [25].

relations.quote: Note that this paper has comprehensively extended our previous work [1] in terms of both theoretical parts (e.g., Sections IV and V) and evaluations (e.g., Sections VI-B, VI-C and VI-E).
relations.why: The paper states it extends its own prior conference work with additional theory and evaluations.

relations.quote: One representative type of approach is built on DMP [13], [14], [15], where unit quaternions were used to represent orientation and different reformulations of DMP were developed to ensure proper quaternions over the course of orientation adaptation.
relations.why: These DMP-based orientation methods are cited as prior approaches that cannot adapt to nonzero angular velocity, motivating the new method.

relations.quote: Another solution of learning orientation was proposed in [16], where GMM was employed to model the distribution of quaternion displacements so as to avoid the quaternion constraint.
relations.why: This GMM-based orientation method is cited as addressing reproduction but not adaptation, a gap the current work fills.

relations.quote: In contrast to [16] that learns quaternion displacements, the Riemannian topology of the S3 manifold was exploited in [17] to probabilistically encode and reproduce distributions of quaternions.
relations.why: The paper contrasts its approach with Riemannian S3 modeling in [17], which lacks via-point and angular-velocity adaptation.

relations.quote: As a recently developed framework, KMP [8] exhibits several advantages over state-of-the-art approaches:
relations.why: The paper builds its learning formulation on kernelized movement primitives (KMP).

relations.quote: In comparison with DMP [5] and TP-GMM [7], that focus on target adaptations, KMP is capable of adapting trajectories towards arbitrary desired points (e.g., start/via/end- points).
relations.why: The paper compares its KMP-based method against DMP and TP-GMM, which are limited to target adaptation.

relations.quote: Unlike DMP and ProMP [6] that rely on explicit definition of basis functions, KMP employs the kernel trick to alleviate the definition of basis functions and thus allows for convenient extensions to the learning and adaptation of demonstrations consisting of high-dimensional inputs.
relations.why: ProMP is cited as relying on explicit basis functions, whereas the proposed kernel approach avoids this for high-dimensional inputs.

relations.quote: It is well known that robot trajectories should be smooth in order to facilitate the design of controllers as well as the execution of motor commands [20], [21].
relations.why: These works are cited to motivate adding angular acceleration or jerk smoothness constraints.

relations.quote: In many previous work, human and robot motions are encoded by taking time as input (e.g., DMP was used in [31] and ProMP in [32]).
relations.why: The paper contrasts its high-dimensional-input approach with prior time-driven human-robot collaboration methods.

relations.quote: 11Readers are suggested to refer to [35] for GMM sampling.
relations.why: This reference is used for the GMM sampling technique that selects input points for high-dimensional learning.

relations.quote: Differing from [19], in our framework (see Section V), each demonstration comprises a high-dimensional varying input trajectory and a robot trajectory
relations.why: The paper contrasts its high-dimensional input learning with [19], which uses time sequences plus contextual states.

relations.quote: Interestingly, some recent works on exploiting the covariance of trajectories and optimal control were reported, e.g., uncertainty-aware controller [11] and minimum intervention controller [39].
relations.why: These works are cited as related uses of trajectory covariance and optimal control that could integrate with the proposed framework.

sections.summary: Imitation learning is promising for transferring human skills to robots, but Cartesian orientation learning remains difficult because quaternions must obey constraints and must support via-point/end-point adaptation, angular velocities, high-dimensional inputs, and smoothness. The paper positions an analytical solution against prior work and summarizes its contributions in Table I.
sections.title: Motivation and Contributions: Orientation Learning in Cartesian Space
